common_name: Carmelo Walnut (UC Davis Late-Leafing Persian Walnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile loam; Carmelo leafs out relatively late in spring, which helps the developing flowers avoid damage from late frosts common in interior valley orchard sites.

directions: Carmelo is a University of California walnut release valued for its very large, well-filled nuts and light kernel color, harvesting slightly later than Chandler on a vigorous, spreading tree. Like other UC Davis Persian walnut selections, it leafs out relatively late in spring, which helps the developing catkins and pistillate flowers avoid damage from late frosts common in interior valley orchard sites. Plant in deep, well-drained loam in full sun with a compatible pollenizer, and expect the first meaningful nut crop several years after grafted trees are established. Space trees widely, since mature Persian walnuts develop broad canopies that shade out understory plantings.
sources: University of California, Davis — Walnut Improvement Program

common_name: Tulare Walnut (Early-Bearing UC Davis Persian Walnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained, fertile loam; train young trees to a strong scaffold structure early, since Tulare's early-bearing habit can produce weak, lateral crotch angles if left unpruned.

directions: Tulare is an early-bearing University of California Persian walnut selection named for the San Joaquin Valley county where much of the state's walnut industry is concentrated. Trees begin cropping earlier in their life than many later-maturing commercial cultivars, producing a large, thin-shelled nut with good kernel quality, though careful framework training when young helps offset a tendency toward weak-angled lateral branching. Give it deep, well-drained soil in full sun and a compatible pollenizer for a consistent crop, and expect nuts to mature in the same general September harvest window as other California Persian walnuts.
sources: University of California, Davis — Walnut Improvement Program

common_name: Solano Walnut (Early-Season UC Davis Persian Walnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained soil; site away from frost pockets, since Solano's comparatively early leafing can expose young growth to spring cold.

directions: Solano is an older University of California Persian walnut release grown chiefly for its early harvest window, ripening well ahead of standard-season cultivars like Chandler and Howard. The tree bears reliably on a spreading, moderately vigorous framework, though its once-wide use in the Sacramento Valley has declined as growers shifted to higher-yielding, disease-tolerant modern releases. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollenizer, and site it away from frost pockets since earlier leafing can expose young growth to spring cold.
sources: University of California, Davis — Walnut Improvement Program

common_name: Meylan Walnut (Grenoble AOC French Persian Walnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Meylan leafs out relatively late, reducing frost damage risk to flowers in cool foothill climates.

directions: Meylan is a traditional French Persian walnut cultivar long grown in the hills around Grenoble as part of the Noix de Grenoble appellation, prized for its large, attractive nut and mild, sweet kernel flavor. It leafs out relatively late in spring, reducing frost damage risk to the flowers in the cool foothill climate where it is traditionally grown. Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, provide a compatible pollenizer, and allow ample room for a broad mature canopy.
sources: Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualite (INAO)

common_name: Fernor Walnut (French Late-Leafing Hybrid Persian Walnut)

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in late winter in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Fernor's late leafing and lateral-bearing habit suit modern, denser orchard spacing better than older French standards.

directions: Fernor is a French walnut selection bred from a Franquette-line cross for late leafing, heavy precocious bearing, and good disease tolerance suited to modern orchard spacing. Its late spring growth start helps flowers escape frost while its lateral-bearing habit, unusual among traditional French cultivars, lets trees crop earlier and more densely than old standards like Franquette. Grow in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollenizer, and expect a heavier, more consistent nut set than older late-leafing French cultivars once trees reach bearing age.
sources: INRAE — French walnut cultivar breeding program

planting.note: Plant bare-root grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; site away from low frost pockets to protect Metcalfe's relatively early spring bloom.

directions: Metcalfe is a cold-hardy Carpathian-strain Persian walnut selection identified in Canada and valued by northern growers for surviving winter temperatures that kill less hardy English walnut cultivars. It produces a medium, thin-shelled nut with good kernel quality on a tree that tolerates the shorter growing seasons of USDA zone 5 better than California-bred selections such as Chandler. Plant grafted trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, provide a compatible pollenizer, and site away from low frost pockets to protect the relatively early spring bloom.

common_name: Colby Black Walnut (Cold-Hardy Wisconsin Black Walnut)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees while dormant in deep, well-drained soil away from garden beds, since black walnut roots exude growth-inhibiting juglone.

directions: Colby is a named black walnut selection identified in Wisconsin and valued by northern nut growers for combining good cold hardiness with respectable kernel quality in a region at the edge of the species' reliable range. Grafted trees bear sooner and more predictably than seedling black walnuts and produce a nut with fair cracking characteristics for the species. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, well away from vegetable gardens and juglone-sensitive plants, and give it the wide mature spacing typical of black walnut.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant grafted trees while dormant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil away from juglone-sensitive garden plants.

directions: Fowble is a named black walnut selection recognized in nut-grower variety trials for a favorable shell-to-kernel ratio that makes cracking noticeably easier than typical wild seedling trees. Grafted trees bear at a younger age and with more consistent annual yield than seedling stock. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and generous spacing clear of juglone-sensitive garden plants.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant grafted trees while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, with ample room clear of juglone-sensitive plants.

directions: McAllister is a named black walnut selection valued among nut growers for vigorous growth and heavy, consistent nut production on a grafted tree. It produces a good-sized nut with kernel quality comparable to other widely propagated named selections, bearing years earlier than an unselected seedling tree. Site it in deep, well-drained soil in full sun with plenty of room clear of gardens sensitive to juglone.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant grafted trees while dormant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, sited well away from juglone-sensitive plantings.

directions: Stambaugh is a named black walnut selection grown for a good percentage of easily extracted kernel meat relative to unselected wild trees, making it a practical choice for home nut growers who process their own harvest. Grafted trees establish bearing several years sooner than seedling black walnuts and crop more uniformly from year to year. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, sited well away from juglone-sensitive plantings.
sources: University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; grow as a multi-stemmed shrub with a genetically distinct pollenizer, since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and self-incompatible.

directions: Bixby is one of the original hybrid hazelnut selections bred in British Columbia by J.U. Gellatly from crosses of the cold-hardy American hazelnut with the larger-nutted European hazelnut, combining winter hardiness with improved nut size over the pure American species. It has served for decades as important parent material in subsequent hybrid hazelnut breeding programs aimed at bringing commercial-scale hazelnut production into cold-winter regions where European hazelnut alone struggles. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a genetically distinct pollenizer, since hazelnuts are wind-pollinated and self-incompatible. Expect a large, multi-stemmed shrub rather than a single-trunk tree, and prune out old wood periodically to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; grow as a multi-stemmed shrub with a compatible pollenizer for reliable nut set.

directions: Faroka is another of J.U. Gellatly's mid-twentieth-century hybrid hazelnut selections, bred in British Columbia to combine the cold hardiness of American hazelnut with better nut size and quality from European hazelnut parentage. Along with sibling selections such as Bixby and Potomac, it has been used repeatedly as breeding stock in later hybrid hazelnut programs targeting the cold-winter Upper Midwest and eastern United States. Grow as a multi-stemmed shrub in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and plant with a compatible pollenizer since hazelnuts do not self-pollinate reliably.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; grow as a multi-stemmed shrub with a compatible pollenizer, since it is not sold as a stand-alone self-fruitful selection.

directions: Potomac is one of the Gellatly-bred hybrid hazelnuts developed in British Columbia from crosses between cold-hardy American hazelnut and larger-nutted European hazelnut, part of the same historic breeding effort that produced Bixby and Faroka. It has been valued mainly as parent stock in later cold-climate hazelnut breeding programs rather than as a widely sold orchard cultivar, though it remains available through specialty nut nurseries. Site it as a multi-stemmed shrub in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollenizer for reliable nut set.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; set a second, genetically distinct hybrid chestnut nearby, since Maraval is not reliably self-fruitful.

directions: Maraval is a European x Japanese hybrid chestnut from the same French breeding program that produced Marigoule and Marsol, grown for its large, glossy nuts and reasonably vigorous growth on a tree that tolerates ink disease better than pure European chestnut. It buds and flowers a little later than some sibling selections, which can help nuts escape early-season frost in marginal sites. Chestnuts are self-incompatible, so plant a second, genetically distinct hybrid chestnut nearby to ensure a full nut set. Harvest burs as they split and fall in early autumn, and collect promptly since fallen nuts spoil quickly on the ground.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; set a second, genetically distinct hybrid chestnut nearby, since Bournette is not reliably self-fruitful.

directions: Bournette is a French European x Japanese hybrid chestnut cultivar developed alongside Marigoule and Bouche de Betizac, selected for good nut size and the blight and ink disease tolerance typical of this hybrid group. It is grown mainly in French orchards for the fresh and processed chestnut trade, where its reliable production complements earlier- and later-ripening sibling cultivars. Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with a distinct pollenizer nearby, since chestnuts will not set a full crop from a single tree. Space trees widely to accommodate their eventual broad canopy.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; set a second, genetically distinct hybrid chestnut nearby, since Marlhac is not reliably self-fruitful.

directions: Marlhac is another member of the French hybrid chestnut group that includes Marigoule and Marsol, selected for a productive, disease-tolerant tree bearing good-sized nuts suited to the fresh and processing chestnut markets. Like its sibling cultivars it carries meaningful resistance to chestnut blight and improved tolerance of Phytophthora ink disease compared with pure European chestnut. Give it deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun and a genetically distinct pollenizer, and expect burs to ripen and split in early to mid autumn.

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; set a second, genetically distinct hybrid chestnut nearby, since Comballe is not reliably self-fruitful.

directions: Comballe is a French hybrid chestnut cultivar noted for vigorous growth comparable to Bouche de Betizac and Marsol, grown in orchards across southern France for its productive, disease-tolerant habit and good nut quality. As with related hybrid chestnut selections, it combines the eating quality and size associated with European chestnut with the blight resistance contributed by its Japanese chestnut parentage. Plant in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with a distinct pollenizer for reliable nut set, and harvest fallen burs promptly in autumn before wildlife or ground moisture damage the nuts.
